title.en: The Moon who could not finish counting

text.en: Chanda Mama, the Moon, tries to count all the stars but always falls asleep or forgets the number. He is upset until the Sun tells him a lovely answer: the number of stars in the sky is the same as the number of children. In this chapter you will read the story, think about things we can and cannot count, use here and there, and write a conversation about the full moon.

Chanda Mama is the Moon. Sometimes he looks round like a circle and sometimes he looks different. One night he started counting the stars, one, two, three, ten, twenty-one, forty-five, ninety-nine, and so on. He yawned and fell asleep before he reached a thousand, and the Sun peeped out and the morning came. When he woke up in the evening he had forgotten where he stopped, and by the time he remembered, the night was over. Night after night he kept counting and kept forgetting the count.
One night Chanda Mama was so upset that he began to cry. The Sun saw his tears and told him not to worry. The Sun said that the number of lovely children is the same as the number of stars in the sky. Chanda Mama was happy. Now the Moon comes out every night, looks at the stars and the children, and smiles.
Some things we can count easily, like children in the classroom, fingers on one hand and pencils in a box. Some things are too many to count, like the stars in the sky, the hairs on your head and children in a whole city. Ask: can I count them in a short time? If yes, they can be counted easily.
The Moon does not look the same every night. It changes from a thin curve to a full round shape and back again. The Moon is seen in the night sky together with stars. In India children call the Moon Chanda Mama, meaning Uncle Moon. You can call him by the name in your language.
Round means shaped like a circle. To count is to say numbers one by one to find how many. Tears are drops of water that come from the eyes when we cry.
We use here for things that are near to us. We use there for things that are far from us. I have a sharpener here in my pencil box, because the box is near me. The crayons are there in the big box across the room, because they are far from me. We are here on the Earth and the Moon is there in the sky.
Children come out on a full moon night and talk about how big and bright the Moon looks. One says a grandfather says the full moon looks very beautiful. Another says her mother has a camera for the picture. They decide to stand together and take a photograph, saying the Moon is so big and bright.

problem.en: Choose here or there: This is my bench. I sit ___ with my friends.

text.en: The bench is near me; I am pointing at it.
So we write: I sit here with my friends.

why.en: There would be for something far away.

problem.en: Sort: pencils in your box, hairs on your head. Which can be counted easily?

text.en: Pencils in a box are only a few.
Hairs on the head are too many.
So pencils can be counted easily; hairs are too many.

why.en: Large numbers are hard to count.

prompt.en: Tell the story of Chanda Mama and explain the Sun's answer.

requiredIdeas.en: The Moon tried to count the stars
He fell asleep and forgot the count
The Sun said the stars equal the children

commonMisconceptions.en: The stars were fewer than the children

points.en: Chanda Mama tried to count the stars but always forgot.
The Sun told him the stars equal the children.
Some things can be counted and some are too many.
Here is for near things and there is for far things.
The Moon changes shape through the month.
